insights.claim: The ExtProc gRPC service has no application-level authentication; security relies entirely on transport TLS and platform-level Envoy/network policy enforcement.
insights.reasoning: The ExtProc gRPC server is constructed with optional TLS credentials but no authentication interceptors (grpc.Creds only, no UnaryInterceptor or StreamInterceptor for auth). Any client with network access to port 9004 can send ExtProc callouts. In production, this is mitigated by Envoy being the only expected caller and by Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, but the absence of application-level auth is an architectural trade-off worth tracking.

insights.claim: The upstream Dockerfile uses CGO_ENABLED=0 (static linking) with a distroless base image, which is incompatible with FIPS check-payload validation requirements.
insights.reasoning: FIPS check-payload requires dynamically linked Go binaries (CGO_ENABLED=1) and OpenSSL in the container image. The upstream build explicitly sets CGO_ENABLED=0 and uses gcr.io/distroless/static:nonroot which lacks OpenSSL. Downstream RHOAI builds must override BASE_IMAGE (to UBI) and build flags to achieve FIPS compliance. The configurable build args (BASE_IMAGE, LDFLAGS) provide the override mechanism.

insights.claim: The ExtProc server generates self-signed TLS certificates at runtime, creating a trust bootstrap challenge for production deployments.
insights.reasoning: The TLS certificate is generated at each server startup using CreateSelfSignedTLSCertificate with a 10-year validity. This means Envoy must be configured to skip certificate verification when connecting to the ExtProc service, or the platform must inject trusted certificates via a different mechanism. The self-signed approach simplifies deployment but weakens the transport security guarantee.
